brief: Twelve checks for a customer-support agent need a home, either in a layer of the evaluation pyramid or in production monitoring once the agent is live.
Place each check where it belongs. Ask what it costs to run, what it observes and how often it can run.

buckets.label: Deterministic checks
buckets.description: The base of the pyramid: exact, cheap checks such as schemas, tool contracts and loop bounds, run on every commit.

buckets.label: Scenario and trajectory evals
buckets.description: The middle of the pyramid: scripted tasks that check the steps the agent took and the tools it called.

buckets.label: End-to-end judgements
buckets.description: The top of the pyramid: human or model-judged scores of whole answers, run before releases.

buckets.label: Production monitoring
buckets.description: Online signals from live traffic, watched continuously and wired to alerts or rollback.

items.text: Every tool call's arguments validate against the tool's JSON Schema.
items.explanation: Schema validation is deterministic and costs almost nothing, so it belongs in the base and runs on every commit.

items.text: A scripted planner that never finishes makes the loop stop with a typed step-limit reason.
items.explanation: A unit test of a loop bound needs no real model and always gives the same result.

items.text: The final answer parses against the response schema, with every required field present.
items.explanation: Parsing has one right result, so it is a base check rather than a judgement of quality.

items.text: On a replayed refund ticket, the agent calls get_order before issue_refund and never calls close_account.
items.explanation: This checks the path the agent took through a scripted task, which is a trajectory eval.

items.text: When a knowledge-base search returns EMPTY, the agent asks a clarifying question or escalates instead of answering.
items.explanation: A scripted scenario with a recorded EMPTY result checks the agent's behaviour on that branch without any live system.

items.text: On a replayed multi-turn ticket, the agent finishes within six steps and 20,000 tokens.
items.explanation: Step and token counts over a scripted task describe the trajectory, so this sits in the middle layer.

items.text: A rubric-bound model judge scores 300 golden-set answers for correctness and quotes evidence for each score.
items.explanation: Judging whole answers against a rubric is an end-to-end judgement, costly enough to run before releases rather than on every commit.

items.text: Two support leads blind-review 50 sampled conversations against the written rubric before each release.
items.explanation: Human review is the most expensive judgement, so it sits at the very top and runs on release candidates.

items.text: A pairwise judge compares old and new prompt answers, running each comparison in both orders.
items.explanation: Pairwise judging of whole answers is an end-to-end comparison; swapping the order controls position bias.

items.text: The hourly rate of conversations handed to a human, with an alert when it rises 3 points above the weekly baseline.
items.explanation: This is an online signal from live traffic, watched continuously rather than run against a fixed set.

items.text: Thumbs-down rate and reopened-ticket rate per prompt version, read from live conversations.
items.explanation: These come from real users after release, so they are production monitoring signals.

items.text: Cost per conversation and p95 latency per release, with automatic rollback when a guardrail threshold is crossed.
items.explanation: Guardrail metrics on live traffic drive automatic rollback during canary and full rollout.
